title: Self-Evolving Visual Agent via Margin Reward

paper.title: Self-Evolving Visual Agent via Margin Reward
paper.abstract:
Abstract Visual agents that interleave reasoning with tool invocation have posed a promising direction for multimodal tasks.
However, learning effective tool invocation usually relies on curated question–answer pairs or expert demonstrations at scale, which are expensive to acquire. In this study, we propose Marvo, a simple-yet-effective self-evolution approach that enables learning tool invocation from unlabeled images.
Marvo consists of two agents: (1) a challenger that generates question-answer pairs from unlabeled images, and (2) a solver that learns tool invocation by solving questions through reinforcement learning.
To encourage effective tool invocation, a good training question should be difficult enough to warrant tool use, yet remain within the solver’s capabilities.
To this end, we introduce a margin reward to the challenger, defined as solver’s performance difference with and without access to tools.
With the margin reward, we create an adaptive curriculum that encourages the solver to learn effective tool invocation.
Across benchmarks covering agentic reasoning, visual search, mathematical, and general real-world reasoning, Marvo improves average accuracy by up to 7.1% — demonstrating margin reward as a preferred way to scale question complexity without human supervision. Code would be released at https://github.com/YWenxi/marvo .

Marvo consists of two agents: (1) a challenger that generates question-answer pairs from unlabeled images, and (2) a solver that learns tool invocation by solving questions through reinforcement learning. To this end, we introduce a margin reward to the challenger, defined as solver’s performance difference with and without access to tools. With the margin reward, we create an adaptive curriculum that encourages the solver to learn effective tool invocation. Across benchmarks covering agentic reasoning, visual search, mathematical, and general real-world reasoning, Marvo improves average accuracy by up to 7.1% — demonstrating margin reward as a preferred way to scale question complexity without human supervision. Code would be released at https://github.com/YWenxi/marvo . 1 Introduction Visual agents have extended the capabilities of multimodal models by interleaving reasoning with tool invocation ( OpenAI, 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . Instead of producing answers solely from an initial visual observations, these agents have already invoked tools to acquire rich evidence, process visual information, and use the feedback to guide subsequent reasoning. This interaction offers a promising approach to multimodal tasks, but requires agents to learn effective tool invocation–they have to determine which tool is useful and how to incorporate its output into the reasoning process. Existing approaches learning these behaviors usually rely on curated question–answer pairs through human supervision or expert demonstrations ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Hong et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026b ) . Such supervision provides task objectives or examples of successful tool use, but is expensive to be collected at scale. Expert demonstrations require constructing suitable interaction trajectories, while question–answer supervision requires identifying meaningful questions and establishing answers. These challenges motivate learning with zero data ( Huang et al., 2026 ) or unlabeled data. Yet converting this potential into useful supervision requires a mechanism for producing valuable tasks and questions, particularly, for visual agents that largely depend on tool invocation. The value of a training question depends not only on its difficulty, but also on whether tools help the solver to correctly answer it. On the one hand, questions that the solver can answer without tools provide little incentive to acquire tool-use behaviors. On the other hand, questions that remain beyond the solver’s capabilities even with tools offer limited opportunities to learn from successful interactions. Useful questions should therefore occupy a region between these extremes: they should pose a challenge beyond the solver’s unaided reasoning while remaining solvable with tool invocation. Moreover, this region depends on the solver’s current capabilities and may shift as the solver improves. A productive training curriculum should track this changing relationship between question difficulty and tool utility. In this study, we propose Marvo, a simple yet effective self-evolution approach that enables visual agents learning tool invocation from unlabeled images (Fig. 1 a). Marvo consists of two agents with complementary roles. A challenger generates question–answer pairs from unlabeled images, and a solver learns to answer the generated questions through reinforcement learning with access to tools (Fig. 1 b). The challenger supplies training tasks, while the solver’s performance provides feedback about their learning values. This interaction allows the training curriculum to adapt to the solver, reducing dependence on a fixed collection of manually curated tasks. To guide the challenger toward questions that promote tool invocation, we introduce a margin reward , which measures solver’s performance difference with and without access to tools. A larger margin, i . e . i.e. , performance difference, indicates that tool access enables the solver to answer a question more successfully than it could through unaided reasoning. Questions that are easily answered in both settings, or remain unsuccessful in both, receive little reward from this objective. Trained with the margin reward, the challenger is encouraged to generate questions that expose opportunities for useful tool invocation. This reward connects question generation directly to the behavior we seek to improve. Optimizing question difficulty alone can favor tasks that the solver cannot solve, while optimizing tool-assisted success alone can favor tasks that do not require tools. The margin reward instead measures the solver’s relative benefit from tool access. As this benefit is evaluated with respect to the current solver, the same objective can guide question generation as the solver’s capabilities evolve. The resulting curriculum emphasizes questions for which tools make a practical difference, enabling visual agents to learn effective tool invocation without manually annotated question-answer pairs or expert demonstrations. Across a diverse suite of benchmarks–11,691 questions spanning agentic reasoning ( Li et al., 2025 ) , visual search Wang et al. (2024b) ; Wu and Xie (2024) , mathematical reasoning Zhang et al. (2024) ; Qiao et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2024a) , and general real-world reasoning–Marvo improves the average accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-7B by 7.1%. Together, these results establish the performance gap between tool-free and tool-augmented answering as a useful signal for generating training questions that improve tool-augmented reasoning. Figure 1: Flowchart of Marvo. (a) Marvo employs an evolution loop between a challenger and a solver, driven by the Margin Reward.
